name: Political bias
statement: People judge the same evidence to be stronger when its conclusion favours their own political side.
meaning: The claim is tested with a matched-information design. Two groups with opposed politics read material that is identical except for the side its conclusion favours, and the gap between their ratings is the bias. Ditto and colleagues define partisan bias as evaluating otherwise identical information more favourably when it supports one's political beliefs or allegiances than when it challenges them. What the design measures is the difference between two evaluations, not the accuracy of either. Two rival hypotheses sit on top of that measure. The asymmetry hypothesis predicts more bias among conservatives, on the grounds that right-wing citizens score higher on needs for certainty and related traits. The symmetry hypothesis predicts the same level on both sides. Which hypothesis the evidence supports is the live argument, and it has been conducted in print by the people on each end of it.

origin.who: Charles G. Lord, Lee Ross and Mark R. Lepper
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their article ran in volume 37, issue 11, pages 2098 to 2109, and was read in full here from the scanned reprint at fbaum.unc.edu. A total of 151 undergraduates answered an in-class questionnaire on capital punishment, and 48 were brought back two to four weeks later, 24 proponents and 24 opponents. Each read one purported study confirming and one disconfirming the deterrent effect of the death penalty, and rated how well each was conducted and how convincing it was. On the difference between the two convincingness ratings the analysis of variance gave a main effect of initial attitude, F(1, 44) = 32.07, p < .001. Taber and Lodge's two experiments on affirmative action and gun control arguments, with 126 and 136 Stony Brook students, are the political version most often cited in between. Ditto and colleagues excluded that paper from their meta-analysis because the arguments the two sides read differed in content rather than being matched.

evidence: Ditto and colleagues meta-analysed 51 experimental studies with 18,815 participants, all using the matched-information design on American samples. Their searches returned more than 1,500 articles, chapters and dissertations. Forty-eight articles met all four inclusion criteria, and the 51 studies in the final set came from 38 articles, 42 of them published and 9 unpublished. Mean overall partisan bias was r = .245, 95% CI [.208, .280], p < .001, and the effect cleared significance in 39 of the 51 samples. Split by side, liberals gave r = .235 and conservatives r = .255, 95% CI [.205, .304]. The difference between the two was r = .009, p = .55, 95% CI [-.020, .038]. The liberal interval appears twice in the manuscript read here and the two do not agree, .192 to .296 in the text and .192 to .276 in Table 2, so the table value is the one printed above. Guay and Johnston put the same question to two national survey experiments. Their 2018 Lucid study recruited 2,085 US adults and analysed the 1,816 who passed two attention checks. The probability of correctly interpreting numeric evidence rose by 10 to 20 percentage points when the evidence favoured the respondent's own side. In their second experiment, judgements of a study's sample size and of its warrant for causal conclusions moved by 0.15 to 0.30 standard deviations in the same direction. A second sample, also of 1,816 US adults, drawn from the 2018 Cooperative Congressional Election Study, repeated the pattern.

examples.text: A report showing crime falling under the current government is called solid by its supporters and thin by its opponents, and both sides have read the same pages. The gap between the two verdicts is the measure, and neither verdict is the accurate one by default.

examples.tag: The sample size that only matters sometimes
examples.text: A reader waves through a survey of two hundred people when the result suits them and asks pointed questions about the sample when it does not. The scrutiny is genuine. What switched it on was the conclusion rather than the method.

A councillor's travel claim is described as an administrative oversight by her own party and as a scandal by the other, on identical paperwork. The paperwork is the matched information, and the difference is what the design is built to catch.

replication.headline: The bias repeats across topics, samples and study designs at r = .245. Whether it is larger on the right is disputed, and the meta-analysis reporting no difference has been attacked on its inputs.
replication.detail: Ditto and colleagues found the overall effect significant in every subgroup of all five moderator variables they coded. Published studies gave r = .266, p < .001 against r = .139, p = .003 for unpublished ones, QB = 6.35, p = .012, with both differing from zero. Publication status did not move the left-right difference, which was r = -.001, p = .95 in published studies and r = .054, p = .11 in unpublished ones. Funnel-plot regressions gave a slope of -.12, p = .42 for overall bias and -.01, p = .97 for the difference. By topic the overall effect ran from r = .192 on abortion to r = .334 on environmental policy, with capital punishment at r = .248 and gun control at r = .210. The 95% prediction intervals are wide. Overall bias runs from 0.003 to 0.486 and the conservative-minus-liberal difference from -0.175 to 0.175, which the authors read as true effects varying from study to study and the difference running in both directions. Guay and Johnston reproduced the bias on two national samples and write that they find little evidence for the asymmetry hypothesis. That is not a clean null, and their paper says so. Their second study turned up three cases in which one side was more biased than the other. One cleared a local alpha of .05, on judgements of causal warrant with left and right coded by issue position, and it ran in the direction the asymmetry hypothesis predicts. A difference of similar size ran the other way when the same outcome was coded by ideology, and coding by partisanship gave close to zero. The numeracy version of the claim has fared worse. Persson and colleagues ran a preregistered replication of Kahan and colleagues with a pre-specified analysis plan and report no good evidence for motivated numeracy. Yu and Opfer tested 1,000 US adults on Mechanical Turk and did not find a consistent interaction between numeracy and political orientation, reporting OR = 0.69, 95% CI [0.51, 0.92], p < .05 for the crime-increases problem and OR = 0.85, 95% CI [0.64, 1.13], p = .278 for crime decreases. The interaction with prior attitude was there, at chi-square(1) = 49.19, p < .001, and their reading is that the motivation runs through prior belief rather than party.

study.cite: Ditto, P. H., Liu, B. S., Clark, C. J., Wojcik, S. P., Chen, E. E., Grady, R. H., Celniker, J. B., & Zinger, J. F. (2019). At least bias is bipartisan: A meta-analytic comparison of partisan bias in liberals and conservatives. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 14(2), 273-291.

limits: Baron and Jost dispute the symmetry finding on its inputs, in the same issue of the same journal. They argue that the 51 studies were assembled for other purposes, so their issues, procedures and materials were chosen in ways that work against detecting an ideological difference, and they note that null differences were obtained in 41 of the 51 experiments. Their second argument is that the bias may not be a bias. Rating congenial evidence as stronger can be rational for someone who already holds the prior, they cite Bayesian analyses of the paradigm, and they point out that no objective standard of accuracy was set against which these judgements could be scored. Ditto and colleagues grant the first point in part, writing that most of the included studies were not designed to test the symmetry question and that most did not report liberals and conservatives separately, so the authors had to be emailed for the data. They answer that the studies covered issues at the core of political conflict, that they picked designs least open to a Bayesian reading, and that a body of work gathered by researchers with different aims is harder to bend than one built around a favoured hypothesis. Guay and Johnston audited the same 51 studies from outside the exchange. On their coding 20 distinguish politically motivated reasoning from rational updating, 12 of those use a representative sampling frame, 9 of those cover salient and divisive issues, 7 of those are published, and 4 of the 7 come from a single research group and account for 86% of the combined sample size. Their conclusion is that there is less evidence against the asymmetry hypothesis than first appears. The evidence base is American and the studies predate 2019. Ditto and colleagues' own limitations section records that they excluded correlational designs, other experimental designs and other kinds of partisan bias, naming selective exposure and the hostile media effect of entry 205. Baron and Jost's supplemental material, where they set out what they call anomalous outcomes, was not obtained. The submitted version of their commentary read here carries an abstract sentence the published abstract drops: that in 7 of the 10 studies showing an asymmetry it was conservatives who were more biased. That count rests on a review-stage manuscript and on no figure in the published article.
misreadings: The commonest error is reading symmetry in this paradigm as symmetry everywhere. Guay and Johnston's respondents who called themselves extremely conservative scored 0.63 standard deviations higher in need for closure than extremely liberal ones, and 0.97 higher on a combined trait index, in the same sample that showed no reliable ideological gap in motivated reasoning. Baron and Jost hold that those domain-general differences are the better guide to American politics. The meta-analytic result is about one measure. Ditto and colleagues discuss selective exposure on its own and call that literature mixed, with several studies finding more of it among conservatives, several finding no political difference and a few finding more among liberals. The second error is treating an average across 51 studies as settling any particular case. The prediction interval for the left-right difference runs from -0.175 to 0.175. The third error is reading bias as irrational. Ditto and colleagues showed 401 Mechanical Turk workers one of four kinds of experimental result and report that more than 90% called each one evidence of biased judgement, falling to a range of 83% to 93% once they adjusted for possible demand characteristics. One of the four results concerned the sex of an essay's author rather than politics. That records what people call bias rather than answering the normative question Baron and Jost raise. The fourth is folding motivated numeracy into the replicated core. That is a separate claim, about quantitative skill amplifying the bias rather than curbing it, and two later tests did not find it on political identity. Accusations of political bias are themselves partisan. Ditto and colleagues asked 951 visitors to YourMorals.org how well the word biased described the average Democrat and the average Republican, and Democratic respondents named Republicans while Republican respondents named Democrats.

sources.text: Ditto, P. H., Liu, B. S., Clark, C. J., Wojcik, S. P., Chen, E. E., Grady, R. H., Celniker, J. B., & Zinger, J. F. (2019). At least bias is bipartisan: A meta-analytic comparison of partisan bias in liberals and conservatives. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 14(2), 273-291. Read in full, twice to the same checksum, from the author manuscript at osf.io/xyq7b, whose own title page reads 'in press'. The published article is closed at SAGE, which returned a Cloudflare challenge to every request on 21 September 2026, and the only open copies Unpaywall lists are submitted versions at the Durham repository, which returned the same challenge. The published abstract at Europe PMC agrees with the manuscript on 51 studies, over 18,000 participants, r = .245, .235 and .255. The confidence intervals, the prediction intervals, the moderator table and the counts of 18,815, 48, 38, 42 and 9 are read off the manuscript only.

Baron, J., & Jost, J. T. (2019). False equivalence: Are liberals and conservatives in the United States equally biased? Perspectives on Psychological Science, 14(2), 292-303. The published article is closed at SAGE, which returned a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026, and the first author's copy at sas.upenn.edu returned 403. Read instead from the manuscript posted at sites.uci.edu, stamped 'For Review Only', manuscript ID PPS-18-005.R2, submitted 18 May 2018. The count of 41 of 51 is read from that manuscript and not from the published text. The supplemental material was not obtained.
